# 0. Why Music Has Structure

Music may feel like cultural invention, but its foundations come directly from:

* **physics** (vibration & overtones)
* **mathematics** (simple ratios → stable intervals)
* **geometry** (how chords relate in space)
* **perception** (why tension & release feel natural)

This set of notes follows how these ideas build into scales, modes, triads, tuning, harmonic motion, and practical musicianship.

# 1. Sound, Overtones, and Generating Intervals

## 1.1 The harmonic series

Every musical tone contains multiple frequencies vibrating together.
These frequencies occur at integer multiples:

> **f, 2f, 3f, 4f, 5f, …**

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="harmonic-series"}
[Interactive figure: the first eight modes of a vibrating string. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

Important resulting intervals:

* **Octave**: 2:1
* **Perfect 5th**: 3:2
* **Perfect 4th**: 4:3

These are the first *highly consonant* intervals.
They are stable because their waveforms align with minimal beating.

## Hearing consonance as an absence of beats

Two tones whose frequencies are close but not equal interfere: the sound swells and fades at their *difference* frequency. For a pure ratio like 3:2, the overtones of the two notes land exactly on top of each other, so there is nothing to beat. Mistune the interval and the overlapping overtones start to wobble.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="beats"}
[Interactive figure: overtone spectra of two notes and the beating between them. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## 1.2 Stacking perfect 5ths → the Pythagorean scale {.compact}

If we repeatedly multiply by 3/2 and fold results into one octave:

$$
f \times (3/2)^n \bmod 2
$$

we generate the **circle of fifths**.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="fifths-circle"}
[Interactive figure: stacking perfect fifths around a one-octave pitch circle. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

Selecting seven fifths in order gives the familiar diatonic notes.
This is the origin of the **Pythagorean scale**.

## Triads emerge automatically

The overtone ratios 4:5:6 produce a **major triad**.
Thus, consonant chords are *not invented* — they are discovered within the harmonic series.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="triad-456"}
[Interactive figure: harmonics 4, 5 and 6 forming a major triad. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# 2. Tuning Systems and the Need for Temperament

## 2.1 Why tuning is impossible to perfect {.compact}

Stack twelve perfect 5ths:

$$
(3/2)^{12} \neq 2^7
$$

This mismatch is the **Pythagorean comma**.
As a consequence:

> **We cannot tune all intervals perfectly at once.**

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="comma"}
[Interactive figure: the error accumulated by twelve pure fifths. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## 2.2 Equal Temperament (ET) as the compromise

ET divides the octave into 12 equal ratios:

$$
2^{1/12}
$$

Its benefits:

* every key sounds the same
* transposition and modulation become seamless
* geometric relationships between notes become uniform

Downside:
none of the intervals except the octave are perfectly pure.

| Interval | Pure ratio | Pure (cents) | ET ratio | ET (cents) | ET − pure |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Minor 3rd | 6:5 | 315.6 | 1.1892 | 300 | −15.6 |
| Major 3rd | 5:4 | 386.3 | 1.2599 | 400 | +13.7 |
| Perfect 4th | 4:3 | 498.0 | 1.3348 | 500 | +2.0 |
| Perfect 5th | 3:2 | 702.0 | 1.4983 | 700 | −2.0 |
| Major 6th | 5:3 | 884.4 | 1.6818 | 900 | +15.6 |
| Octave | 2:1 | 1200 | 2 | 1200 | 0 |

Fifths and fourths are off by only 2 cents, which is barely audible. Thirds and sixths are off by 14–16 cents, enough to beat clearly (you can compare them in [6.2](#intonation-on-a-violin)).

# 3. Tetrachords and Scale Construction

## 3.1 Modern pedagogical tetrachords {.compact}

We adopt four patterns (not ancient Greek ones):

* **Ionian:** W–W–H
* **Dorian:** W–H–W
* **Phrygian:** H–W–W
* **Lydian:** W–W–W

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="tetrachords"}
[Interactive figure: the four tetrachords on a keyboard, with their whole and half steps. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

A **scale** = tetrachord + whole step + tetrachord.

## 3.2 Two fundamental generative sequences {.compact}

### A. The Moving Window

Take a major scale and begin on each degree:

> Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="mode-window"}
[Interactive figure: a window sliding along the white keys to show each mode. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

This is the **modal perspective** familiar today.

---

### B. Combining Tetrachord Types

Scale = lower tetrachord + upper tetrachord.

Examples:

* Ionian + Ionian → **Major**
* Lydian + Ionian → **Lydian**
* Ionian + Dorian → **Mixolydian**
* Dorian + Phrygian → **Minor**

This reveals the **architectural symmetry** inside the diatonic system.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="tetrachord-matrix"}
[Interactive figure: every combination of lower and upper tetrachord. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# 4. Geometry of Chords and Voice-Leading

## 4.1 The Tonnetz (triads as geometric objects) {.compact}

Arrange pitches so:

* horizontal direction = fifths
* diagonal directions = major/minor thirds

Then each major/minor triad forms a small triangle.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="tonnetz" data-mode="explore"}
[Interactive figure: a clickable Tonnetz lattice. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

This gives a **visual map of harmonic space**.

## 4.2 Smooth voice-leading as geometric proximity

Chord changes sound smooth when their notes move short distances.
On the Tonnetz, close-position triads are literally **adjacent**.

This shows why certain progressions feel natural — they follow short geometric paths.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="tonnetz" data-mode="progression"}
[Interactive figure: chord progressions animated as paths on the Tonnetz. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# 5. The Resolution Principle

## 5.1 Why dominant → tonic resolves

Three factors:

1. **Leading tone** moves by the smallest melodic interval
2. **Chordal 7th** falls downward
3. **Overtones of V** overlap with **overtones of I**, reducing beating

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="resolution"}
[Interactive figure: the voices of G7 resolving to C, and the overtones the two chords share. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## 5.2 Tension as “distance”

* Consonant chords = small distances in harmonic space
* Dissonant chords = larger distances
* Harmonic motion = navigating this space efficiently

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="tonnetz" data-mode="walk"}
[Interactive figure: a Tonnetz walk with the voice movement of each step. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

# 6. Application to Violin (Minimal but Essential)

## 6.1 Tetrachords = Left-Hand Frames {.compact}

Each tetrachord corresponds to a repeatable 4-finger pattern.
Mastering these patterns improves:

* shifting
* scale fluency
* intonation consistency

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="violin-frames"}
[Interactive figure: the four tetrachord frames on a violin fingerboard. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::

## 6.2 Intonation on a violin

String players often tune:

* 4ths & 5ths **pure** for resonance
* 3rds **just** when harmonizing
* melodic intervals **expressively**, not rigidly ET

Understanding the underlying acoustics helps maintain good intonation.

::: {.mf-widget data-widget="intonation"}
[Interactive figure: pure and equal-tempered intervals compared by ear and in cents. It needs JavaScript.]{.mf-noscript}
:::
